summary: For ages 6–8, teach children to justify material choices by the PROPERTY the job needs, not by habit or appearance: glass for windows because it is transparent and waterproof; boots from waterproof, flexible plastic/rubber; wood for a chair because it is hard and rigid. Move from naming a property to using it as a REASON, comparing two candidate materials head-to-head for one job, running the reasoning both ways (why this suits / why an alternative fails), and recognising that many objects need SEVERAL properties at once so 'best' means best-on-balance. Absurd-material provocations (chocolate teapot, glass hammer) and inventor case studies (Dunlop, Macintosh, McAdam) make the property→purpose reasoning explicit. Aligns to DfE KS1 Y2 'Uses of everyday materials' and NGSS 2-PS1-2.
misconceptions: Choosing a material by familiarity or appearance ('cups are usually plastic') rather than by the property the job needs.
Believing there is one 'best' material for everything (often metal or plastic), instead of best-for-this-purpose.
Failing to link the property to the function — naming a material as suitable without saying which property makes it so.
Ignoring that objects often need SEVERAL properties at once, so judging on a single property and missing trade-offs.
Assuming a material's suitability is fixed by what it 'is' rather than reasoned from tested behaviour (a Y2→Y5 fair-test bridge).

activities.title: Kit out the job: choose a material and see if it works
steps: Pick an everyday object with a clear job — a rainy-day coat, an umbrella, a saucepan, a window, a boot.
Choose a material for it from a small set (e.g. paper, plastic, glass, cardboard, metal).
State out loud, before testing, which property you think matters and why you picked that material.

Observe or act out what happens when the object is used: pour water on the coat, let 'rain' hit the window. Any test involving heat (a saucepan near a hob, warm water on chocolate) is run by an adult as a demonstration, or acted out in pretend play — children do not hold materials near real heat.
Compare the result to your prediction: did the paper coat let the rain soak through? Did the plastic coat bead the drops off? Name the property that decided the outcome.
Watch the absurd choice (an adult pours warm water into a chocolate teapot) and describe what goes wrong and why.

For the window, compare glass (you can see out AND rain stays out) with a sheet of metal (rain stays out but it is dark — you cannot see through it), with cardboard (dark, and it goes soggy and lets water through), and with no material (wet) to discover that some jobs need TWO properties at once.
activities.insight: The right material rescues a job and the wrong one visibly lets it down, so a property is a REASON for a choice, not just a label; some jobs demand more than one property at once.

activities.title: Real objects and their earning property (reveal scene)
steps: Look at real everyday objects or an illustrated home/street scene (window, coat, saucepan, book, wellies).
For each object, name the one property that earns its material its job — e.g. 'wellies — plastic — WATERPROOF so your feet stay dry'.
Then consider 'what if it were made of paper?' and say why that would fail.
Handle or examine the real objects where possible to connect the property word to how the material behaves.
activities.insight: Every object around us was made from a material chosen for the property its job needs, and swapping in the wrong material reveals why that property mattered.

activities.title: Which is better for this job — and why? (head-to-head)
steps: Take one job (a raincoat, a drinking cup, a hammer) and two candidate materials.
Decide which material is better for that job and SAY the property that makes it win.
Run the reasoning in reverse: explain why the other material would be a poor choice.
Sort a small set of materials into 'suitable' and 'unsuitable' for a named job, giving a property reason for each.
Spot the silly material in a set (e.g. a glass hammer among metal tools) and explain what would go wrong.
activities.insight: Judging two materials against each other for one purpose forces you to weigh a property against a need, which is stronger than judging a single material in isolation.

activities.title: The inventor's problem (material choice as problem-solving)
steps: Hear a short story of an inventor who solved a real problem with a material: Charles Macintosh and the waterproof coat, John Dunlop and the air-filled (pneumatic) rubber tyre, John McAdam and road surfacing made of layers of crushed stone.
Say what problem the inventor faced and which property of the material they chose solved it.
Take on a design brief in role — e.g. 'I need a coat that keeps the rain out' — choose a material and justify it, answering 'why not paper?' follow-up prompts.
Keep turns short; speak or act out the justification rather than writing long answers.
activities.insight: Choosing a material is a real human problem-solving act: an inventor matches a material's property to the job that needs doing.

checkQuestion: Say: 'Wellington boots are made of rubber or plastic. Someone says it's just because boots are always made of that. What's the REAL reason we pick that material for boots — what does the material need to do?' Then: 'I want to make a teapot. Would glass, metal or chocolate be a bad choice — and why?'
checkAnswer: Matches the property to the purpose: boots are plastic/rubber because they are waterproof AND flexible (bend as you walk, keep feet dry); a chocolate teapot fails because chocolate melts with hot water. Reasons from the property the job needs, not from habit or looks.
